reason: A spathe limb can curve forward or inward. The examples are correct.
Sepals are often mottled with red or purple.
A corona lobe is not a stalked organ. 'Sessile' describes the corona or its appendage, so the part is wrong.
'Oblate' fits an anther outline only occasionally. One example is about the apical appendages, not the anther. A rule would need to tell anther from appendage.
Corona lobes can spread or diverge.
Pinna size is compared along a frond ('basal pinnae largest'), so increased size fits.
Ploidy and chromosome number are routinely given for the whole plant, as in 'Plants octoploid'.
Paleae are often oblanceolate.
The examples measure sinuses, grooves and fissures, not the corolla lip. The depth belongs to the sinus or cleft, so the part reading is wrong.
Fruit valves can be glabrous.
The examples all describe the margin ('margins 1/2 involute'), not the staminode. A rule would need to assign margin statements to the margin or to the organ.
A capsule can be rectangular in outline. Other examples are about exothecial cells, which are the wrong part. A rule would need to separate cell shape from organ shape.
A spike base or tip can be attenuate.
Fruits can be concavo-convex or plano-convex, for example in flattened fruits.
Midveins can be ciliate.
Nutlets can be flattened.
Inflorescences can be cup-shaped, as in Euphorbia cyathia or cup-like clusters.
A stem base can be hispid.
Fruit valves can be rugose or rugulose.
The example is about the dark colour of the stalk continuing into the pinna base. That is colour of the stalk, not brightness of the pinna.
Bracts can be hastate.
A seed coat can be warty or verrucose.
The examples say the midnerves are raised, so the bearer is the midnerve, not the whole involucral bract.
The hairiness is described for the lamina surface (adaxial, abaxial). The epidermis can carry the indumentum in this scheme.
Involucral bracts or their apices can be flattened.
A leaf lobe can itself be cleft into secondary divisions.
Phyllaries are often fringed, including pectinately.
The ovary can be inconspicuous (rudimentary or sunken), but one example is about grooves. A rule would need to separate the ovary from other parts.
Thorns or spines can be filiform, thread-like or hair-like.
Leaf blades can be concavo-convex.
A tree crown can be columnar.
Fruit valves can be keeled. The negated examples are handled by negation.
Bracts can be mottled.
Tubercles can be short, so decreased length fits.
Inflorescence axes such as the rachilla can be fragile.
Scale leaves and sheaths are often papery.
The examples describe spurs and other organs as curved, not the short shoot. The part is wrong.
A rostellum or its arms can be slender.
Corolla lobes can be tapered, mostly at the base or toward the tip.
Tepals can be delicate or fragile.
'Lax' cells in mosses mean thin-walled and wide-meshed. PATO 'loose' means something else, so the reading is wrong.
Achenes can be persistent or deciduous. Some examples are about the beak or calyx, but the pair itself is meaningful.
Perianth bristles can be retrorse, with backward-pointing barbs.
Terminal buds can be conical.
Turions can be axillary or terminal, so position fits.
Trichomes can be reflexed or deflexed.
Inflorescence branches and axes can be tomentose.
Achenes or their beaks can be bristly.
The abaxial lamina surface can be floccose.
Anthers can be cream-coloured.
This is a comparison ('wider than the leaves'), not a quality. It belongs to width with a comparison rule.
A perianth or its margin can be entire.
Achenes can be elongated.
The adaxial tepal surface can have a colour.
Petals can be mottled.
Tepals can be mottled.
Fruits can be tasteless or insipid.
Involucral bracts can be curved or incurved.
Paleae can be hispid, for example along the keels.
The examples are 'laminar gland dots', which is the position of glands. It is not a quality of the leaf lamina, so the reading is wrong.
